hook: This metal melts in your hand
caption:
This metal melts in your hand.

Gallium (Ga, element 31) melts at just 29.8 °C, so the warmth of your palm turns a solid lump into a silvery puddle. Mendeleev predicted it before it was discovered and called it eka-aluminium, the same story your Class 10 periodic classification chapter tells. Today it lights up LEDs and sits in the chips inside your phone.

question: Sodium reacts violently with water. Chlorine is a toxic gas. Together they make?
explanation: Sodium chloride, NaCl: table salt. Two dangerous elements, one thing you eat every day.
caption:
A metal that fizzes in water + a toxic greenish-yellow gas = something on your dinner table.

Lock in your answer before the reveal. Then the why: sodium hands one electron to chlorine, and the two ions that form are held together by an ionic bond. That's a big chunk of Class 10 Metals and Non-metals in one reaction.

question: Which element is the most electronegative of all?
explanation: Fluorine, 3.98 on the Pauling scale. It pulls shared electrons harder than any element.
caption:
A periodic-trends favourite in school exams and NEET/JEE prep. Lock in your answer before the reveal.

The trick so you never forget: electronegativity rises as you go right across a period and up a group. Head for the top-right corner of the table, skipping the noble gases.

caption:
Iron floats on this metal.

Mercury (Hg, element 80) is a liquid at room temperature and about 13.5 g/cm³ dense, much denser than iron at 7.9, so an iron nail floats on top. Its symbol comes from hydrargyrum, meaning water-silver. Its vapour is toxic, so this one stays in the lab.

question: Which gas makes up most of the air you breathe?
explanation: Nitrogen, about 78% of air. Oxygen is only about 21%, and argon nearly 1%.
caption:
Sounds easy. Lock in your answer before the reveal.

After the reveal, a bonus: the same gas is pumped into chip packets to keep the chips from going rancid, because it doesn't react with the oil the way oxygen does. Yes, that's in your Class 10 textbook too.

caption:
This metal defines one second.

Since 1967, one second has officially been 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from caesium-133 atoms. Atomic clocks count them, and satellite navigation like GPS depends on clocks this precise. Caesium (Cs, element 55) is also an alkali metal so reactive that it explodes in water.
